prompt: What reaches the browser from `src/types.ts`?
hint: A type exists only while you write the code.

choices.text: A small object describing each type, for checks at run time
choices.why: TypeScript has no run-time presence; nothing checks a value against `Session` in the browser.

choices.text: The two type names, as strings
choices.why: Not even the names survive; `import type` is removed whole.

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Right. Types are removed before the file is sent; they guide the editor and the compiler.

choices.text: The whole file, unchanged
choices.why: The browser cannot run TypeScript syntax; it gets JavaScript.

prompt: Why does `week.ts` turn a day into a `Date` at noon UTC rather than at midnight?
hint: Think of a computer in São Paulo reading midnight UTC.

choices.text: So that no time zone moves the date to the day before or after
choices.why: Right. Midnight UTC is still the previous evening in São Paulo; noon is the same day everywhere.

choices.text: Noon is when the sessions start
choices.why: The data has no times at all, only days.

choices.text: `Date` refuses a time of midnight
choices.why: `Date` accepts midnight; the trouble is which day it lands on locally.

choices.text: It makes the arithmetic faster
choices.why: Speed is the same; correctness is the reason.

prompt: `inWeek` compares dates with `>=` and `<=` on strings. Why does that work here?
hint: Look at the order of the parts in `YYYY-MM-DD`.

choices.text: Text order is time order in this format
choices.why: Right. Year, then month, then day, each padded to its width.

choices.text: JavaScript converts both strings to dates before comparing them
choices.why: It compares them as text, character by character.

choices.text: TypeScript rewrites the comparison for strings
choices.why: TypeScript removes types and leaves comparisons as they are.

choices.text: It works only for dates in the same month
choices.why: It works across months and years, which is why the format was chosen.

prompt:
What does Vite turn `

Week of {formatWeek(monday)}

` into before the browser sees it?
hint: The section asked the development server for the translated file.

choices.text: An HTML string that is inserted into the page
choices.why: No HTML string is built; the result is a call that returns an object.

choices.text: A `<template>` element
choices.why: JSX has nothing to do with the HTML template element.

choices.text: A call to `_jsxDEV` with `"p"` and its children
choices.why: Right. The tag becomes the first argument and what sat between the tags goes under `children`.

choices.text: Nothing, because browsers read JSX
choices.why: No browser reads JSX; it has to be translated first.

prompt:
A component returns `

…

…

` with nothing around them, and the compiler refuses. What is the smallest fix?
hint: A function returns one value.

choices.text: Put a comma between the two elements, as in an array literal
choices.why: Between tags a comma is text; it would not make two values into one.

choices.text: Return the first and render the second from `main.tsx`
choices.why: That splits one component's output across files for no reason.

choices.text: Change the `<h2>` into a `<div>`
choices.why: There would still be two roots, and the heading would be lost.

choices.text: Wrap them in `<>…</>`
choices.why: Right. A fragment groups them into one value and adds no element to the page.

prompt: Because `class` is a reserved word in JavaScript, JSX spells the attribute `___`.
hint: It is a property name of DOM elements.

prompt: You need `if (sessions.length === 0) … else …` inside the braces of some JSX. Why does that not compile?
hint: What can stand where an argument goes?

choices.text: An `if` is a statement, and braces hold an expression
choices.why: Right. Braces become an argument, and only an expression produces a value there.

choices.text: JSX supports `if` only inside a fragment
choices.why: No position in JSX accepts a statement; fragments change nothing about that.

choices.text: The compiler cannot see variables declared outside the component
choices.why: It sees them; the problem is the kind of code, not its scope.

choices.text: `length` is not allowed in JSX
choices.why: Any expression is allowed, `length` included.

prompt: Which of these is a component, as far as JSX is concerned?
hint: JSX reads the first letter.

choices.text: `<section>`
choices.why: Lowercase: an HTML element, passed as a string.

choices.text: `<CourseCard>`
choices.why: Right. A capital letter passes the function itself.

choices.text: `<courseCard>`
choices.why: Lowercase, so React asks the browser for a `courseCard` element, which does not exist.

choices.text: `<course-card>`
choices.why: A name with a dash is treated as a custom HTML element, not as your function.

prompt: After the one-letter mistake `<courseCard`, what did the page show?
hint: `look` printed the console first, then the snapshot.

choices.text: A blank page and Vite's error overlay
choices.why: Nothing failed to compile, so there was no overlay.

choices.text: The full screen, unchanged
choices.why: The cards were gone; only the console said why.

choices.text: Three cards with lowercase titles
choices.why: The casing of the component's name has nothing to do with its text.

choices.text: The heading and the week, with the three course cards missing
choices.why: Right. Unknown elements drew empty, and the errors were only on the console.

prompt: Why does this course export every component except `App` by name?
hint: Compare `import { CourseList }` with `import App`.

choices.text: Default exports are slower to load
choices.why: Both kinds load the same way.

choices.text: React refuses default exports for components other than the root
choices.why: React never sees how a module exported a function.

choices.text: A named import cannot be renamed by accident
choices.why: Right. And an editor can find every use of the name.

choices.text: Vite needs named exports for the overlay
choices.why: The overlay works with either.

prompt: In the planner, in which direction do props move?
hint: The figure of the tree has arrows pointing one way.

choices.text: From a parent down to its children
choices.why: Right. `App` hands its data to the components that draw it.

choices.text: From a child up to its parent, when the child finishes rendering
choices.why: A child has no way to pass a prop upwards; lesson 4 shows how it asks its parent to change something.

choices.text: Between siblings, through the parent's `key`
choices.why: `key` is not a prop at all, and siblings never pass props to each other.

choices.text: Both ways, as in two-way binding
choices.why: Two-way binding is what some frameworks offer; React keeps one direction.

prompt: `CourseCard` ran `course.name = course.name.toUpperCase()`. Why did the compiler accept it?
hint: What does the type say about who may change the object?

choices.text: Because the line was inside a component
choices.why: Components have no special permission; the type is the question.

choices.text: Because `tsc` does not check `.tsx` files
choices.why: It checks them; the next section shows it refusing one.

choices.text: Because strings are always mutable
choices.why: Strings are immutable; the line replaced the object's property with a new string.

choices.text: Because `Course` says nothing about the field being read-only
choices.why: Right. The rule that props are read-only is React's agreement, not something this type enforces.

prompt: Why did the capitalised names appear on every card, and stay, rather than only in the card that ran the line?
hint: Was `course` a copy?

choices.text: Each card ran the line on the same objects from `sample.ts`
choices.why: Right. The card changed the data itself, for every reader, from then on.

choices.text: React copies props into every child that renders after the change
choices.why: React does not copy props; it passes the same objects along.

choices.text: Vite reloaded the page with the new text
choices.why: Nothing was saved to a file; the change happened in memory.

choices.text: The CSS turns headings into capitals
choices.why: `index.css` has no `text-transform`; the text itself changed.

prompt: A component, given the same props, returns the same JSX and changes nothing outside itself: it is a ___ function.
hint: The word the section uses for a function of its inputs only.

prompt: What does `Card` receive as `children` when `CourseCard` renders it?
hint: Whatever sits between the opening and closing tags.

choices.text: The `title` prop, repeated
choices.why: `title` arrives separately; `children` is what was between the tags.

choices.text: Every `CourseCard` on the screen
choices.why: Each `Card` receives only what its own parent wrote inside it.

choices.text: The paragraph with the count and the minutes
choices.why: Right. The parent decides what goes in.

choices.text: An empty array, until lesson 4 adds state
choices.why: Children have nothing to do with state.

prompt: You need a card with a red border for an error message. Following this section, what do you write?
hint: The answer is not inheritance.

choices.text: A class `ErrorCard extends Card`
choices.why: Function components do not extend each other; that is the inheritance this section replaces.

choices.text: A copy of `Card.tsx` with the border changed and every caller updated
choices.why: A copy works and drifts; composition avoids it.

choices.text: A change to `index.css` that makes every card red
choices.why: That changes every course card too.

choices.text: An `ErrorCard` that renders `<Card>` with the message as children
choices.why: Right. One component wraps another and decides what goes in.

prompt: How many minutes did the first screen say were done in the week of 19 October?
hint: The numbers lesson 1 promised.

prompt: `App` passed `monday={19}`. What did the development server do?
hint: Vite removes types without checking them.

choices.text: It refused to serve the page and showed the overlay
choices.why: The overlay is for errors Vite meets while transforming; a type error is not one.

choices.text: It printed the type error in its terminal and served the page anyway
choices.why: The development server never ran the type checker, so it had nothing to print.

choices.text: It served the page, which said "Week of Invalid Date"
choices.why: Right. The page drew, and was wrong.

choices.text: It converted 19 to a string
choices.why: Nothing converts it; `formatWeek` got a number and made an invalid date.

prompt: Put the places that can catch a wrong prop in the order you meet them, from the earliest.
hint: The earliest is while you are still typing.
items: The editor underlines it as you type
`npm run build` refuses it before `vite build` runs
A user meets the wrong page

prompt: Why did `npm run build` stop without running `vite build` at all?
hint: Read the script: `tsc -b && vite build`.

choices.text: Vite saw the error and gave up
choices.why: Vite never started.

choices.text: npm stops every script at the first warning
choices.why: npm runs the script; the shell's `&&` decides.

choices.text: The build needs the development server stopped
choices.why: The two can run at the same time.

choices.text: `&&` runs the second command only when the first succeeds
choices.why: Right. `tsc -b` failed, so the build never began.

prompt: With `monday={19}`, the week line was wrong and `80 of 195` was still right. What does that tell you about testing a change by looking at the page?
hint: Where did the numbers come from?

choices.text: A page that renders proves the props are right
choices.why: This page rendered with a wrong prop.

choices.text: The numbers were cached from the previous render
choices.why: Nothing was cached; they were computed from `MONDAY`.

choices.text: TypeScript fixed the totals but not the date
choices.why: TypeScript changes nothing at run time.

choices.text: Looking only shows what the wrong value reached
choices.why: Right. `App` computed the week itself, so the mistake touched only the line that read the prop.

prompt: Match each file to its job in the first screen.
hint: One of them imports nothing from React.

pairs.right: Which days fall in a week, and the totals
A frame with a heading around anything
One card per course, each with its sessions
Choosing the week's sessions and handing them down

prompt: Which of these would the compiler refuse? Choose every one.
hint: Compare each with the props types.

choices.text: `<CourseCard course={course} />`
choices.why: Refused: `sessions` is required by `CourseCardProps`.

choices.text: `<Card title="Spanish">text</Card>`
choices.why: Accepted: a string is a `ReactNode`.

choices.text: `<WeekSummary monday="2026-10-19" sessions={[]} />`
choices.why: Accepted: an empty array is a valid `Session[]`.

choices.text: `<Card title={42}>text</Card>`
choices.why: Refused: `title` is a string.

hint: 26 October is a Monday.
